title: Time: connecting words and expressions
subtitle: prior to, subsequently, throughout, at some point
summary: Connect events in time with more formal and precise expressions than before, then and while.

lesson.heading: One thing before another
lesson.text: **Prior to** is formal and written. **Previously** is fairly formal; in speech we often say *before that*. **Earlier on** is fairly informal. **Formerly** is used when something has changed its name or state.

examples.text: I had written to her **prior to** meeting the committee.
It was nice to be in Venice. **Previously** I'd only been to Rome.
I was in the office from 2.30. I was out **earlier on**.
The street is now called Treetop Avenue. **Formerly** it was Hedge Lane.

lesson.heading: In the meantime
lesson.text: **In the meantime** and **meanwhile** mean 'between now and the time of the event we have just mentioned'. They fill the gap between two points.

examples.text: Dinner will be ready in about an hour. **In the meantime**, relax and have a drink.
The technician arrives at four. **Meanwhile**, we'll work on paper.

lesson.heading: Things happening at the same time
lesson.text: **(At) the very time** and **the very moment** are stronger and more precise than *as* or *just as*. **Simultaneously** means two things started and ended at exactly the same time.

examples.text: She was entering at **the very moment** I was leaving.
**During** the war, she lived in Dublin.
**Throughout** the war, they remained in the city.

left.label: during
left.text: **During** does not say how long within the period. It could be a day or a week of it.
examples: She had a lot of phone calls **during** the day.

right.label: throughout
right.text: **Throughout** means from the beginning to the end of the whole period.
examples: I was in Oslo **throughout** the summer.
**Throughout** the war, they remained in the city.

lesson.heading: One thing after another
lesson.text: These are rather formal words for sequencing events, common in letters of application and reports. **Following** = after; **subsequently** = at some time after that; **thereafter** = after that point.

examples.text: **Following** my first visit to Beijing, I read several books about China.
I **subsequently** decided to take a six-month course in Mandarin Chinese.
I revisited China on several occasions **thereafter**.
The government removed the price regulations and the **immediate** result was a 10% price rise.

lesson.heading: Time when
lesson.text: **The moment** and **the minute** mean 'as soon as'. **The time (that)** points to one particular occasion; **on that occasion** is the more formal version.

examples.text: **The moment** I saw his face I knew I'd met him before.
**The minute** she put the phone down it rang again.
I stayed in that hospital **the time** I broke my leg.
I met Paula at Mark's wedding. **On that occasion** she was with a different man.

lesson.heading: Non-specific time expressions
rows: at some time further on in a process
**At a later stage** we can discuss the detailed arrangements.
at an unspecified time in the future
**At some point** we will have to replace our computers.

lesson.text: Prior to, following, subsequently and thereafter belong to formal writing; earlier on and the minute belong to everyday speech.

exercises.prompt: Match each expression with its meaning.

pairs.right: used to be called or be

exercises.prompt: Dinner will be ready in about an hour. ___, relax and have a drink.
exercises.explanation: In the meantime / Meanwhile = between now and the event just mentioned.

exercises.prompt: ___ going to Manchester, Laura was in Paris.
exercises.explanation: Prior to is a formal, written way of saying before.

exercises.prompt: On Sunday she had a lot of phone calls ___ the day.
exercises.explanation: During does not say how much of the day the calls took.

exercises.prompt: She had been away for a week. ___, she had lots of emails to deal with.
exercises.explanation: Subsequently = at some time after that; fairly formal.

exercises.prompt: She was in Glasgow on the 15th. ___, she had been in Manchester.
exercises.explanation: Earlier on = before then. It is fairly informal.

exercises.prompt: ___ her visit to Nick, she saw a bad accident on the motorway.
exercises.explanation: Following = after; typical of formal writing.

exercises.prompt: The ___ she put the phone down it rang again.
exercises.explanation: The moment / The minute = as soon as.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite the words in bold: 'The two committees were meeting **at exactly the same time**.'
exercises.explanation: Simultaneously = starting and ending at exactly the same time.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite the words in bold: 'I will contact you **at a time I can't specify** to arrange a meeting.'
exercises.explanation: At some point = at an unspecified time in the future.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite the words in bold: 'I emailed James and got a reply **straight away**.'

exercises.statement: Gunilla says: 'I was in Oslo throughout the summer.' This means she spent the whole summer in Oslo.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Throughout means from the beginning to the end of the period.

exercises.statement: Gunilla says: 'Josep visited me during that time.' This means Josep spent the whole summer in Oslo.
exercises.explanation: During does not say how long, so Josep probably spent just part of it there.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression point backwards, forwards, or to the same time?
